source.title: Learning with Noisy Labels Revisited: A Study Using Real-World Human Annotations
source.authors: Jiaheng Wei; Zhaowei Zhu; Hao Cheng; Tong-Liang Liu; Gang Niu; Yang Liu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text including appendix is present.
record.tranche_reason: Measures memorization of correct and wrong labels over training on real human and synthetic label noise, bearing on V6 with a different noise setting and measure than random labeling.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates human-annotated and matched synthetic label noise, not completely random labels or unstructured inputs. Its comparisons of test accuracy in Tables 2, 3, 8 and 9 concern noisy-label learning methods; they do not measure V1–V5. The paper cites earlier work for the clean-label-first pattern; cited results are not extracted as this study’s own results.
record.test_reason: The clean-label-first ordering is attributed to prior work. The study's own Figure 6 measures confidence-thresholded predictions under human and matched synthetic noise: Definition 2 counts a feature as memorized when any class has probability above 0.95, without requiring agreement with its training label. This does not establish the label-fitting order in V6. No own results test V1–V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' stated memorization conclusion: human and matched synthetic noise yield different behavior, with easier feature memorization under human annotations. Here memorization means confidence above a threshold, not necessarily fitting the assigned label. The broader conclusion is that human noise is instance-dependent and creates additional challenges for noisy-label learning.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains ResNet-34 with cross-entropy on human-annotated CIFAR-N and matched synthetic class-dependent noise, rather than fitting completely random labels; Figure 6 compares memorization curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise setting (aggregate, Random 1, worst) and clean versus wrong label samples are shown separately in Figure 6.

fits_no_version.finding: At a confidence threshold of 0.95, the authors report easier feature memorization under human annotations than under synthetic class-dependent noise with the same transition matrix.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human and matched synthetic label noise produce different trajectories of confident correct and incorrect predictions during training.

record.problems: The memorization trajectories are presented in a figure without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The paper's stated temporal pattern for learning clean before wrong labels is attributed to cited prior work; the text does not explicitly describe that ordering for its own Figure 6 results.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowing with increasing corruption.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep and steadily increasing test error toward chance. Benchmark test accuracies alone do not establish this joint claim.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it preserves true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before fitting noisy labels. The study cites this ordering but does not establish it through its reported confidence-based comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 6's curves are unavailable in the supplied text; axes and captions do not establish their temporal ordering. This prevents an effect verdict and is not evidence that V6 is absent or reversed.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling; near-zero training error and chance test error; unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training time or convergence rate as label corruption changes.
Sweep from clean to completely random labels with training and test error outcomes.
Whether regularization, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting random labels or determine generalization.

The experiment compares human annotation noise with synthetic class-dependent noise, not completely random labels; its figure reports memorization proportions, not a direct test that shared real-data patterns are learned before random labels.
